analysis.one_liner: Sets the federal minimum wage by local cost of living and raises the tipped minimum wage.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2025 with one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor, the bill has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee with no markup, vote, or further action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill replaces the flat $7.25 federal minimum wage with a wage tied to local living costs. The floor would start at 40% of the national average hourly wage for ordinary non-management workers and step up to 50% over two years, then be multiplied by an adjustment from 87.5% to 115% depending on how expensive each metro or rural area is. It would also raise the cash wage employers must pay tipped workers to 30% of the regional minimum, up from the $2.13 federal floor. Because it never got a committee vote, none of this has happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid near the federal minimum, especially in the roughly twenty states where the state minimum is still $7.25, and tipped workers whose cash wage would rise from $2.13 to a percentage of the regional minimum. Workers in expensive metros gain the most because of the 115% adjustment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum-wage and tipped workers in low-wage states

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces the flat federal minimum wage with one set for each metro area or rural region, starting at 40% of the national average hourly wage of private-sector non-supervisory workers and stepping up to 45% after one year and 50% after two years.
Each area's wage is then adjusted by regional price parity, from 87.5% in the cheapest areas up to 115% in the most expensive, so the floor tracks local living costs.
Employers would have to pay tipped workers a cash wage equal to 30% of the regional minimum, replacing the $2.13 federal tipped floor that has not changed since 1991.
The subminimum 'training wage' for young workers would rise from $4.25 an hour to two-thirds of the regional minimum, and the exception would be limited to workers 18 or younger.

The wage would be recalculated every three years, taking the higher of the new calculation or the previous period's wage, so it can rise over time rather than freezing as the current $7.25 has since 2009.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers: restaurants that use the tipped minimum, retail, agriculture, and small businesses in low-wage regions would face higher payroll costs as the floor phases up.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retailers, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: The regional formula means workers in low-cost areas would get a noticeably lower floor than workers in expensive metros; a worker in a cheap rural region would earn roughly 87.5% of the baseline while a worker in the priciest metros earns 115% of it, so the bill gives up the simplicity of one national floor.
The wage only recalculates every three years rather than every year with inflation, so it can again fall behind rising prices between updates.
Employers could still pay teenagers in their first 90 days two-thirds of the regional minimum, so a legal subminimum wage persists for workers 18 and under.

A higher wage floor raises costs for small and independent restaurants and retailers, and some employers respond by cutting hours, staffing, or prices in ways that fall partly back on the same low-wage workers the bill is meant to help.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of workers still earning $7.25 or $2.13 tipped, this is a substantial raise, phased in over two years and tailored so lower-cost regions are not hit with big-city wage levels overnight. The main honest objections are the permanent regional gap in the floor, the slow three-year update cycle, and the retained teen subminimum — real design compromises, but they do not undo the core benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat without a markup or vote ever since.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Fitzpatrick introduced the Fair Wage Act of 2025 in the House on May 15, 2025, with Representative Perez as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day, and the action history shows no further steps — no markup, no vote, no referral to a second committee.
The bill has exactly two cosponsors, one Democrat and one Republican, which is far short of the support needed to force committee action.

Under the bill, the regional minimum would start at 40% of the national average hourly wage of private-sector non-supervisory workers, rise to 45% and then 50%, and be scaled by regional price-parity adjustments between 87.5% and 115%.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet because no vote has occurred. For now, employers in states using the $7.25 federal floor and employers of tipped workers keep paying the current federal minimums unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Wage Act of 2025 and authored its regional cost-of-living minimum wage formula.

for.name: Rep. Perez
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote in the months since it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is bipartisan — one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — but there are no votes in the record, so the partisan shape of the fight is not yet visible.

industries.note: The bill raises the cash wage for tipped employees from $2.13 to 30% of the regional minimum, which is a direct payroll cost for restaurants that currently count tips toward the minimum. Their interest in keeping the tipped floor low runs against the pay of the workers themselves.

industries.industry: Retail, agriculture, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: Where the federal floor is the binding one, payroll for the lowest-paid workers would rise as the regional minimum phases from 40% to 50% of the national average wage. Employers' savings from a low floor come directly out of workers' pay.

analysis.trajectory: With only two cosponsors and no committee action since May 2025, the realistic path is the common one for a first-term House bill: it stays in the Education and Workforce Committee without a markup and expires at the end of the 119th Congress unless the chair schedules it or support grows sharply. Nothing in the record suggests that is happening.
